summary:
East Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, which applies in full to visitors in the province. Private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised under national law, but it carries no protection: Indonesia has no national law prohibiting discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no hate-crime protection on those grounds.

The amended penal code, passed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment on complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in Aceh and South Sumatra does not apply in East Kalimantan. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and bind anyone present within that province, including foreign visitors, and they have been carried out: two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025.

Expression offences are national and a visitor can trigger them. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Official hostility is explicit in national policy. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction, placing it inside national defence policy. A feature published on 14 August 2026 reports that civil society describes conditions as rapidly worsening.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. In July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several cities, including West Java, and no prosecutions of the attackers were reported. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. No incident documentation was found for East Kalimantan itself.
tangentialFactors:
Social attitudes are hostile and measurable. Pew reported in 2025 that 93% of Indonesians view homosexuality as morally unacceptable, and estimated 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023. In the international arena Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

Local regulation diverges by district across the country, so the rules a person encounters depend on where they are. A 2021 Bogor city bylaw addresses same-sex conduct, while a 2020 raid in which a gay transgender couple was released for lack of a regional regulation shows that districts without such a rule reach different outcomes.

For comparison, provinces that do carry their own same-sex criminalisation impose corporal punishment: in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and Aceh's provisions apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.
localsOnly:
Residents of East Kalimantan live under the same national penal code as visitors, and the extra-marital sex provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations because same-sex marriage is not available. There is no national statute shielding residents from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate-crime mechanism keyed to those grounds.

Changing legal gender requires sex reassignment surgery and a court order, and identity documents recognise only 'male' and 'female'; there is no third-gender or X marker. Residents therefore have no route to a document that reflects a non-binary status.

Because subnational rules vary by district, residents in different kabupaten and kota face different local bylaws on LGBTQ+ conduct. A 2021 Bogor city bylaw and the 2020 release of a gay transgender couple for want of a regional regulation elsewhere illustrate how far provincial and district practice diverges.

Residents are also exposed to the wider pattern of mob violence and police operations documented nationally, including the July 2026 attacks on trans women in several cities and the June 2025 villa raid near Bogor, where 75 people were arrested.
outOfScopeNotes:
Penalty reporting for the 2022 penal code provision is inconsistent across sources: national-level reporting cited up to two years' imprisonment, while the source set used here gives up to one year on complaint. The discrepancy is unresolved.

No source in the current inventory documents enforcement, arrests or violence against trans people within East Kalimantan itself, and whether the province or any of its kabupaten has adopted a local regulation addressing LGBTQ+ conduct is not sourced.

Whether the October 2025 presidential decree has been applied through provincial institutions in East Kalimantan is not sourced; the decree is documented at national level only.

Locations of the July 2026 mob attacks are given only as several cities including West Java, with no reporting identifying incidents in East Kalimantan or in the country's eastern provinces.
